This historic combat photograph captures former DEVGRU Red Squadron operator Rob O'Neill (bottom left, with blonde hair) administering IV fluids to exhausted U.S. Army Rangers during the intense search, rescue, and recovery operations following Operation Red Wings in the summer of 2005. 

Operating at high elevations in rugged Afghan terrain pushed even elite forces to their absolute physical limits. Severe dehydration, exhaustion, and relentless heat made basic medical maintenance like intravenous saline administration a daily necessity to keep teams combat-effective. 

During the massive manhunt and recovery mission for fallen Navy SEAL LT Michael Murphy and his reconnaissance team, Naval Special Warfare operators, Army Rangers, and support elements worked side-by-side in treacherous conditions to secure the mountains and bring their brothers home. 

Long before historical milestones or public acclaim, operators on the ground faced grueling, unglamorous days on the ridgelines—managing casualties, combat stress, and severe physical depletion under constant threat.

This rare look shows an Uruguayan military member holding an iconic, combat-proven M1A1 Thompson submachine gun—a weapon that first saw action on the battlefields of World War II over 80 years ago.   

Originally acquired through mid-20th-century U.S. military aid programs, the heavy, milled-steel M1A1 Thompson served as a frontline submachine gun in Uruguay until the mid-1980s, when it was officially replaced by the 9mm Argentine-made FMK-3 submachine gun. 

Rather than melting down or destroying obsolete small arms when new rifles arrive, the Uruguayan military has historically maintained a policy of preserving older weapons in deep-storage armories. Because of this, classic firearms like the M1A1 Thompson, M1 Garand, and M1 Carbine occasionally resurface for specialized familiarity training, reserve exercises, or ceremonial duties. 

Weighing in at roughly 10 pounds unloaded and firing the hard-hitting .45 ACP cartridge at 700+ rounds per minute, the simplified wartime M1A1 design is practically indestructible—proving that good steel and timeless engineering never truly go out of style.

On April 7, 2003, during the fierce opening days of Operation Iraqi Freedom, U.S. Air Force Captain (later Colonel) Kim "Killer Chick" Campbell cemented her place in aviation legend when her A-10 Thunderbolt II took a direct hit over downtown Baghdad—and she refused to bail out.   

While diving below cloud cover to deliver close-air support for pinned-down U.S. ground troops near the Tigris River, Campbell had just finished firing her 30mm GAU-8 Avenger cannon and rockets when a surface-to-air missile slammed into the rear of her Warthog. The blast shredded her horizontal stabilizer, punched over 150 shrapnel holes into the fuselage and right engine cowling, and instantly severed both redundant hydraulic systems. 

As the crippled jet rolled violently left and pitched straight toward the streets of central Baghdad, Campbell knew ejecting meant parachuting directly into enemy hands. In a split second, she flipped the switch to manual reversion—a mechanical backup system of pulleys, cranks, and steel cables that pilots compare to steering a heavy truck with the stick stuck in quick-setting cement. 

Escorted by her flight lead, Lt. Col. Richard "Bino" Turner, Campbell muscled the battered Warthog for an hour over 300 miles back to Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait. Rather than ejecting over friendly territory as the flight manual suggests, she elected to land the aircraft with no hydraulic flight controls, no speed brakes, and no normal steering—setting it down so smoothly that the wing's chief of safety remarked she landed it better with no hydraulics than most pilots do with all systems operational. She was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross for her extraordinary airmanship under fire.
That's cold... But smart!

A comprehensive U.S. Army medical study examining the brutal physical toll of Ranger School has revealed that female soldiers who complete the course finish in better overall physiological condition than their male counterparts, experiencing significantly less hormonal disruption and preserving a higher percentage of lean muscle mass. 

Conducted by researchers from the U.S. Army Research Institute of Environmental Medicine (USARIEM) and published in the Journal of Applied Physiology and Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, the study tracked male and female candidates through the 61+ days of severe caloric deprivation, minimal sleep, and non-stop physical exertion across the Darby, Mountain, and Swamp phases. 

While male soldiers entered and exited the course with higher absolute strength and power, their bodies experienced a far steeper physiological crash. Men lost significantly more total body mass and lean muscle tissue, whereas female candidates metabolized fat stores more efficiently—preserving their fat-free muscle mass to a much greater extent and exhibiting fewer extreme drops in metabolic and endocrine hormone markers. 

Lead researcher James McClung noted that while both sexes suffered identical declines in sleep quality and physical output metrics over the two-month course, female physiology proved remarkably resilient against prolonged starvation and multi-stressor exhaustion, concluding: "An elite warfighter is an elite warfighter. It doesn't matter what your sex is."

Can a dedicated 26-Marine Scout Platoon fully replace the legendary Scout Sniper platoons and give infantry commanders the ultimate eyes and ears on the modern battlefield? 

The U.S. Marine Corps’ newest primary infantry career field—the 0315 Marine Scout—is officially in effect, establishing a dedicated reconnaissance and surveillance pipeline on the heels of the Corps' controversial decision to phase out traditional Scout Sniper platoons in 2023.   

Previously treated as an additional skillset rather than a standalone career path, Marine Scouts now hold their own Primary Military Occupational Specialty (PMOS 0315) alongside riflemen (0311), machine gunners (0331), and mortarmen (0341). 

These specially trained Marines populate a 26-Marine Scout Platoon inside each infantry battalion—as well as scout teams within Light Armored Reconnaissance (LAR) battalions. Each scout team also embeds a certified Joint Fires Observer (JFO) capable of calling in devastating air and artillery strikes on high-value enemy targets. 

Trained in advanced fieldcraft, stealth, unmanned aerial systems, and assured long-range communications, 0315 Scouts are built to slip ahead of the main force, map routes to the objective, and extend an infantry battalion's sensing capabilities across contested littoral and inland environments.

U.S. service members and commanders could soon be required to complete annual "religious liberty training" following sweeping recommendations from a White House-directed commission aimed at expanding faith-based protections across the armed forces.   

Chaired by Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick and former cabinet secretary Ben Carson, the federal Religious Liberty Commission issued a comprehensive report urging the Pentagon to implement annual training on religious accommodations, protect personal religious expression in the ranks, and integrate "religious liberty impact assessments" into operational planning. 

The panel also called on the military to produce an updated "spiritual fitness guide" and elevate the role of military chaplains—building on recent Pentagon moves to establish an Office of Religious Affairs and restore troops who previously sought religious exemptions from vaccine mandates. 

While Pentagon officials stated they welcome the recommendations as a vital step toward protecting First Amendment conscience rights for those in uniform, critics and some service members argue that adding another mandatory annual training block could spark debate over how different faiths are represented across a diverse force.

Cody Alford lived at the sharp end of the spear. He deployed on multiple combat tours to Iraq and Afghanistan, leading sniper teams, kicking doors, and surviving under relentless enemy fire.

He earned the Bronze Star with Valor. But the battlefield takes a toll that body armor can't stop.

Hundreds of close-range breaching blasts, artillery concussions, and IED shockwaves tore through his brain. By the end of his career, Cody was suffering from severe Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI), neurological breakdown, vestibular failure, and crippling PTSD.

His body and mind were shutting down.

When the uniform came off, the silence was louder than gunfire. Cody found himself stripped of his identity, struggling through neurological fog, and fighting just to function each day.

But instead of surrendering to the spiral, Cody chose to wage a new war—the war for his own mind and life.

Through intense neuro-rehabilitation, discipline, and honest self-examination, he rebuilt himself from the inside out.

He shared his entire journey on The Shawn Ryan Show, giving millions of veterans permission to acknowledge their invisible combat injuries and seek real healing. Today, through his platform We Are The They, he mentors people to break through mental barriers and conquer their internal battles.

The scars you can't see are often the hardest to heal.

True strength isn’t staying unbroken. True strength is picking up the pieces and forging yourself into something stronger.

Electronic Warfare & Decoy Nodes: Emitting false radar signatures and jamming enemy targeting networks to draw hostile fire away from manned destroyers and aircraft carriers.

The U.S. Army has officially issued a major policy directive (MILPER 26-350) granting automatic promotion to Staff Sergeant (E-6) for any Sergeant (E-5) who successfully completes and graduates from the U.S. Army Drill Sergeant Academy.

Supporters argue this is well-earned recognition for taking on one of the most stressful, burnout-heavy duties in the armed forces.

For the first time since the Korean War, the U.S. Army is actively preparing for the grimmest reality of large-scale combat: digging temporary mass graves directly on the battlefield.

During recent high-intensity readiness exercises at Fort Liberty, North Carolina, combat engineers from the 20th Engineer Brigade, soldiers from the 3rd Corps Sustainment Command, mortuary affairs specialists, and Army chaplains trained with heavy bulldozers and excavators to establish standardized field burial sites.

The metrics from the exercise are chilling:

Standardized burial trenches for 20 fallen soldiers can be excavated in just 75 minutes.

Using eight bulldozers and four military excavators, an engineering unit could temporarily inter the remains of up to 2,400 soldiers within a single 24-hour window.

For the past 20 years in Iraq and Afghanistan, the U.S. military enjoyed complete air dominance. Every fallen warrior was treated with reverent custody and flown directly home to Dover Air Force Base within days.

But Pentagon war games for a potential clash against a near-peer adversary—such as China or Russia—reveal a brutal reality:

Contested airspace, anti-ship missiles, and cyber-disrupted logistics could sever supply lines for weeks.

Immediate air repatriation would be physically impossible, and casualty counts could reach thousands in days.

Frontline units would be forced to temporarily inter fallen soldiers in the dirt to maintain positive identification, prevent disease, and protect remains until the combat zone can be secured for repatriation.

As Sergeant 1st Class Delbert Ruede stated during the drills: "If we went to war tomorrow, we would be making this up as we went along. What we are doing here is taking a scientific, field-tested approach so that we can maintain positive control and respectfully care for our fallen."

Practicing the unthinkable is the starkest sign yet of how seriously military planners view the threat of major war.

Is the military being responsibly realistic about near-peer warfare, or is this a chilling warning of where global tensions are heading?

The Pentagon, U.S. Army Criminal Investigation Division (CID), and U.S. Cyber Command are officially investigating a wave of simultaneous, catastrophic freezer meltdowns across military base commissaries as a suspected foreign cyberattack.

In recent weeks, commercial refrigeration systems at commissaries across multiple major military installations including Fort Huachuca and bases across several states inexplicably malfunctioned at the exact same time. The sudden temperature overrides thawed massive freezer rows, spoiling hundreds of thousands of dollars in groceries and leaving military families with empty shelves.

Federal investigators quickly connected the dots: the incident closely mirrors a sophisticated cyberattack in France that remotely hacked and shut down environmental cooling controls across more than 350 commercial supermarkets.

While spoiled commissary food might sound like an annoyance on the surface, cybersecurity and military intelligence analysts warn that this is a classic asymmetric infrastructure probe:

Operational Technology (OT) Infiltration: Hostile nation-state hacking groups (such as China or Russia) are actively testing their ability to breach the industrial control systems and software running U.S. military installations.

The Wartime Threat: If foreign hackers can remotely shut down cooling systems in base grocery stores, the exact same networked SCADA vulnerabilities can be used during a conflict to overheat classified supercomputer data centers, ruin temperature-sensitive missile propellant in munitions depots, and destroy military medical blood and vaccine banks.

Gray-zone cyber warfare isn't coming in the future—it's already hitting domestic bases inside our own borders.

Is targeting grocery stores and base infrastructure an early warning of a massive cyber conflict, or are military networks too vulnerable to basic commercial hacking?

Major Jeffrey R. Calero was an elite Special Forces detachment commander with Company C, 1st Battalion, 20th Special Forces Group (Airborne).

Originally from Puerto Rico and raised in New York, Calero was brilliant and driven. He earned his mechanical engineering degree from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (RPI) before choosing a life of service, earning his Green Beret in 2001.

As an officer, Calero believed in leading from the front. He never asked his men to take a step he wouldn't take first.

On October 29, 2007, while leading an Operational Detachment Alpha (ODA 2132) on a high-risk dismounted combat patrol through hostile terrain in Kajaki, an improvised explosive device (IED) was triggered.

Major Calero was killed in action, giving his life in defense of his team and his country. He was 34 years old.

Awarded the Bronze Star Medal and Purple Heart, Major Calero represented the highest standard of leadership, quiet professionalism, and selfless sacrifice within the Special Forces brotherhood.

A leader walks ahead of his men. A hero lives on in their hearts forever.

March 4, 2002. A 10,000-foot freezing mountain peak in eastern Afghanistan: Takur Ghar.

When a Navy SEAL was thrown from a damaged Chinook into an enemy hornets' nest, Air Force Combat Controller John Chapman volunteered to go back onto that mountain to get his brother back.

As soon as their helicopter touched down, they were hit with RPGs and heavy machine-gun fire. Chapman charged uphill alone through thigh-deep snow, assaulted an al-Qaeda bunker, and neutralized the fighters inside.

While assaulting a second bunker, he was shot multiple times and knocked unconscious. Believed to be fallen, his team was forced to break contact down the mountain.

But John Chapman wasn’t dead.

Sixteen years later, declassified high-definition drone footage revealed the truth: Chapman woke up alone on that freezing peak. Severely wounded and surrounded by dozens of enemy fighters, he refused to quit.

For over an hour, he fought a solo one-man stand from a snow bunker.

When an inbound quick-reaction helicopter carrying 18 Army Rangers flew directly into the ambush zone, Chapman knew they would be shredded.

He made his final choice: he stepped out of his bunker into the open, drawing all enemy fire toward himself to protect the landing helicopter until he was mortally wounded.

His solo stand saved the lives of every man on that incoming bird.

In 2018, Master Sergeant John Chapman was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor—the first Air Force special operator to receive it since Vietnam.

Deep behind enemy lines during Operation Red Wings, a 4-man Navy SEAL reconnaissance team was surrounded by over 50 Taliban fighters on the steep cliffs of Mount Sorkh Sar.

Outnumbered and taking heavy fire from three sides, Lieutenant Michael P. Murphy knew his team wouldn't survive without emergency air support. But the steep mountain terrain blocked their radio signal.

Knowing it was almost certain death, Lieutenant Murphy made a choice.

He deliberately walked out of cover into the direct line of enemy machine-gun fire to reach an open rock ledge where his satellite phone could get a signal.

As he made the transmission to headquarters to give their coordinates, an enemy bullet tore through his back. He dropped the phone, picked it back up, finished the call, signed off with "Thank you, sir," and continued firing at the enemy until he was mortally wounded.

His sacrifice allowed the extraction helicopter to deploy, saving the life of Marcus Luttrell. Lieutenant Murphy was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor.

November 21, 2010. Marjah, Helmand Province, Afghanistan.

Lance Corporal Kyle Carpenter and his best friend, Lance Corporal Nick Eufrazio, were manning a rooftop machine-gun post when an enemy grenade landed directly next to them behind the sandbags.

In combat, a grenade gives you about three seconds. Most people run.

Kyle Carpenter dove.

Without a second of hesitation, Carpenter lunged forward and threw his body directly onto the live explosive, using his chest and Kevlar to shield Nick from the lethal blast.

The grenade detonated underneath him.

The explosion shattered his jaw, collapsed his lung, took his right eye, broke dozens of bones, and filled his body with shrapnel. When the medevac team loaded him onto the helicopter, he had no pulse. He was pronounced dead on arrival.

But Kyle Carpenter refused to die.

He flatlined three separate times on the operating table, endured over 40 surgeries, and spent two and a half years in the hospital rebuilding his body piece by piece. Both he and his brother Nick survived.

In 2014, he walked into the White House to receive the Medal of Honor, becoming the youngest living recipient in the nation.

He gave his face, his eye, and his youth so his brother could go home to his family.

Semper Fidelis isn't just a motto. It's a promise kept in blood.

The Navajo were honored first, in 2001 — but they were never the only ones. Choctaw and Cherokee soldiers had spoken the first coded words in 1918. Comanche men hit Utah Beach on D-Day. Twenty-seven Meskwaki from one small Iowa tribe served together in North Africa. Hopi, Lakota, Pawnee, Creek, Seminole and more — in all, members of more than thirty tribes carried their languages into America's wars, and most of them went to their graves officially unrecognized.

The Code Talkers Recognition Act of 2008 set out to fix that, and on November 20, 2013, in the United States Capitol, it happened: Congressional Gold Medals were presented honoring twenty-five more tribes' code talkers, with silver medals for the individual men and their families. Old soldiers in red caps and yellow scarves — and widows and grandsons standing in for those who never lived to see it — finally heard a grateful nation say their names out loud.

The men in this photograph, Navajo elders in their eighties and nineties, sat for honors that arrived two generations late. Their verdict on the long wait was the same grace they'd shown in 1945: no bitterness, just pride. The medals were gold. The men were better.

For twenty-three years, America's greatest battlefield secret was guarded by the men's own silence. 🇺🇸

When the code talkers came home in 1945, their officers gave them one final order: tell no one. Not their wives, not their children, not anyone — what they had done, and how. The code was still a classified military asset, and so some of America's most remarkable veterans went back to their farms, ranches and oil fields carrying a story they were forbidden to share.

They kept that silence until 1968, when the Pentagon finally declassified the code talker program. Only then — twenty-three years later — could the men explain the strange questions their families had always wondered about. Slowly, the nation began to understand: President Reagan proclaimed a National Navajo Code Talkers Day in 1982; in 2001, the surviving Original 29 received Congressional Gold Medals, and every other Navajo talker the Silver.

The men in this photograph are the elders of that brotherhood in their later years, gathered at their traveling display — the portraits of their fallen friends on the banner behind them — still driving to schools, museums and veterans' events in their nineties to tell the story in person. Every year, there are fewer chairs filled at that table. What they ask of us is simple: remember the code, and remember who spoke it.

This is the full team: the Comanche code talkers of the U.S. Army's 4th Signal Company, 4th Infantry Division — front row, second from right, Charles Chibitty; with him Roderick Red Elk, Simmons Parker, Larry Saupitty, Melvin Permansu, Willie Yackeshi, Wellington Mihecoby, and behind them Morris Sunrise, Perry Noyebad, Ralph Wahnee, Haddon Codynah, Robert Holder, Albert Nahquaddy, Clifford Ototivo and Forrest Tsimpoid, among their brothers of the seventeen.

Recruited from Oklahoma beginning in 1940 and hardened at Fort Benning, Georgia, these men built a Comanche military vocabulary of more than a hundred terms — because their ancient language had no words for things like tanks, bombers or Adolf Hitler, they invented them: Hitler became "Crazy White Man," a tank a "turtle," and a machine gun a "sewing machine." Then they memorized all of it, because in the field, nothing could be written.

On D-Day they hit Utah Beach with the first waves of the 4th Infantry Division and kept the division talking — securely — from Normandy to the heart of Germany. Not one Comanche transmission was ever understood by the enemy. Seventeen men did that. When the Army finally told the story decades later, America learned that one of its most effective secret weapons in Europe had been a language spoken around Comanche campfires for a thousand years.

Todd Corbin - Navy Cross Recipient in the face of danger, most would run toward safety. Yet, when then-Lance Cpl. Corbin was faced with such a decision, he ran toward peril and possible death – braving intense enemy fire to help injured comrades.

Corbin, a medium tactical vehicle replacement driver, and his unit were stationed in the Al Anbar province to help secure and stabilize the volatile area. They had just finished several days of routine patrol on May 7, 2005, and were returning to the Haditha Dam when they got the call.

A platoon from their battalion was under attack on the east side of the Euphrates River and needed support to block the insurgents' retreat. Corbin's team – a quick reaction force (QRF) – quickly responded to the call. As the QRF crept toward the attack site, there was an unnatural stillness in the air.

“There was no one out, nothing moving,” Corbin later told the Marine Corps Times.

With every nerve on alert, the QRF kept driving toward the ambush site, knowing there were injured Marines that needed them. Suddenly, a vehicle laden with IEDs sped toward the convoy and blew up between two of the Humvees. Another blast followed as enemy fighters began firing upon the group.

The swift attack devastated Corbin's team – three of the four vehicles were severely damaged, and 11 of 16 Marines were injured or killed. Taking control of the situation, Corbin immediately repositioned his vehicle between the insurgents' fire and the wounded Marines. As he radioed in the situation, he began directing a counter-attack.

As those that could returned fire, Corbin began recovering dead and wounded personnel and moving them toward safety. Running through the line of fire, Corbin grabbed his wounded patrol leader and threw him over his shoulder. He then sprinted back to his Humvee, firing at enemies as he ran. Corbin ran back and forth several times through the kill zone, moving everyone he could out of the withering fire and loaded them into his vehicle.

Arming every able Marine with as much ammunition and weapons as they could hold, Corbin drove his severely damaged Humvee through the kill zone toward the battle aid station. Even injured, the Marines were a deadly force to be reckoned with. Insurgents continued to pelt the rumbling truck with mortars and small-arms fire, but the Marines made it to safety.

Corbin's quick actions ensured that no Marines were killed after that initial attack. For his leadership, Corbin was awarded the Navy Cross on April 12, 2006.

Charles Joyce Chibitty was a Comanche kid from near Medicine Park, Oklahoma, when the Army came looking for men who spoke his language. He became one of just seventeen Comanche code talkers assigned to the 4th Infantry Division — a tiny band of men carrying an outsized secret into the biggest invasion in history.

On the morning of June 6, 1944, Chibitty came ashore at Utah Beach on D-Day, among the very first code talkers to put the language to work in Europe. From that beachhead across France and into Germany, the Comanche talkers sent their coded messages — tank became "turtle," a bomber a "pregnant airplane," a machine gun a "sewing machine" — and German intelligence, for all its brilliance, never understood a single transmission.

Chibitty fought through the whole campaign and came home to Oklahoma, where in his later years he became the honored elder of the Comanche code talkers — traveling, teaching, and reminding America that Native men had helped win the war in a voice straight from their own grandmothers' kitchens. Honors found him at last, including the Army's Knowlton Award for intelligence work. When Charles Chibitty died on July 20, 2005, the last surviving Comanche code talker went silent — but the seventeen voices of the 4th Signal Company are part of D-Day forever.

The code talkers did not begin in World War II. They began in France, in 1918. 🇺🇸

In October 1918, during the Meuse-Argonne offensive, the American 36th Division had a deadly problem: German listeners tapped their phone lines at will, and every code the Americans tried was broken within hours. Then an officer overheard two of his own soldiers chatting in Choctaw — and realized he was listening to a language no German on Earth could understand.

Within days, Choctaw soldiers of the 141st Infantry were manning field telephones across the sector, relaying orders for troop movements and artillery in their native tongue. The Germans were stunned into silence. Within twenty-four hours the tide in the sector turned; within seventy-two, the surprised enemy was in full retreat — and American officers were writing reports calling the Choctaw telephone squad one of the cleverest moves of the war.

Nineteen Choctaw men are remembered as the first code talkers — the pioneers whose idea the Navajo, Comanche and two dozen other tribes would carry into the next war. Yet when they came home, their story was buried for decades; most Americans never learned their names in their lifetimes. It took until 2008 for Congress to formally honor them, and 2013 for their gold medals to be struck. This photograph is where the whole legend starts: a group of young Choctaw soldiers, an American flag, and a language that saved lives.

They look like any three young Marines on a troopship in 1945, grinning for the camera with their rifles and gear. In fact, these Navajo code talkers were sailing toward Okinawa — the last and largest battle of the Pacific war — carrying in their heads a code that had frustrated Japan's best intelligence officers for three straight years.

By 1945, more than 400 Navajo code talkers served across the Marine Corps' Pacific divisions. At Okinawa they did what they had done at Guadalcanal, at Tarawa, at Iwo Jima: they turned shouted battlefield chaos into fast, flawless messages the enemy could not read. Everything rode on their voices — artillery fire, casualty calls, ammunition requests, the movements of thousands of men.

None of it was written down. The entire code — hundreds of terms, a full alphabet — existed only in the memory of young men like these three, most of them barely out of their teens, many of whom had been punished in government schools for speaking the very language that now made them irreplaceable. The irony was not lost on them. It was their quiet revenge, and their gift.

Look at those smiles. They knew what they were carrying. Japan never did.

In November 1943, the 2nd Marine Division stormed Betio Island at Tarawa in one of the bloodiest battles in Marine Corps history — more than a thousand Marines lost in just seventy-six hours. Radios failed at Tarawa. Wires were cut, sets drowned in the lagoon, headquarters lost contact with men pinned at the seawall. What could not fail was the code talkers' network: a human chain of voices speaking a language that no amount of enemy listening could unlock. Through them, commanders called down naval gunfire, redirected reserves, and learned where their men still held on.

The young Marine in this photograph has no famous name attached to his picture — and that is exactly the point. The code talkers were not celebrities. They were teenage radiomen who carried the battle's nervous system in their own mouths, island after island, while the world knew nothing about them. Peter MacDonald was born in 1928 in Teecnospos, Arizona, raised in a hogan, speaking Navajo — and when he heard the Marines were looking for code talkers, the fifteen-year-old lied about his age and enlisted in 1944. He mastered the secret code, shipped out with the 1st Marine Division, and served in North China as the war ended, one of the youngest men ever to carry America's most guarded battlefield secret in his memory.

Coming home, MacDonald did something just as remarkable: he got an education. He became an electrical engineer — one of the first Navajo engineers in the country — and worked on advanced missile programs before returning to serve his people. In 1970 the Navajo Nation elected him its Chairman, and he would win four terms, the longest-serving leader in the Nation's modern history — a code talker who had defended his country now fighting for his tribe's water, land and future.

Today, in his late nineties, Peter MacDonald remains one of the last living links to the Original Era of the code talkers — a national spokesman who still travels to tell young people what a handful of Navajo voices did in the Pacific. From a fifteen-year-old who lied to serve, to the leader of a nation: his whole life has been one long act of duty.

REMEMBERING GREEN BERET SSG KYU “Q” CHAY: FALLEN AT THE TIP OF THE SPEAR

Today we honor the ultimate sacrifice of Staff Sergeant Kyu “Q” Chay, a veteran Green Beret assigned to the 1st Battalion, 3rd Special Forces Group (Airborne), who gave his life in defense of freedom on October 28, 2006.

Before there were hundreds, there were twenty-nine. 🇺🇸

In May 1942, twenty-nine young Navajo men — shepherds, students, farmers' sons — walked into Marine boot camp as the first all-Navajo platoon in Corps history. At Camp Elliott in San Diego, they were locked into classrooms with a top-secret order: invent an unbreakable code, from scratch, in their own language.

Working day and night, the 29 built it in layers — a phonetic alphabet (A for "ant," B for "bear") and a dictionary of military terms that grew past 400 words, every one of them memorized, because nothing could ever be written down in the field. In testing, they encoded, sent and decoded a three-line message in twenty seconds. The Marines' best machines took thirty minutes.

Their code went to war across the Pacific and was never broken — the only oral code in modern military history that never fell. By 1945 more than 400 Navajo code talkers were serving, and at Iwo Jima their six networks handled more than 800 messages in the first two days without a single error. Their commanding signal officer said it plainly: "Were it not for the Navajos, the Marines would never have taken Iwo Jima."

In 2001, the surviving members of the Original 29 received the Congressional Gold Medal. The bronze talker on his knees at Window Rock, radio in hand, stands for all of them — twenty-nine young men who turned the language of home into a shield for a nation.

Chester Nez was a shy teenager from the Navajo Nation when Marine recruiters came looking for men who spoke his language in the spring of 1942. He became one of the Original 29 — the first platoon of Navajo code talkers — the men handed an impossible job: build a battle code out of a language that had almost no written form, and build it in weeks.

They did it. An alphabet. Hundreds of memorized words — "iron fish" for submarine, "hummingbird" for a fighter plane, "turtle" for a tank. Nez then carried that code into some of the fiercest fighting of the Pacific war — Guadalcanal, Bougainville, Guam, Peleliu — sending and receiving orders under fire that Japanese codebreakers could hear perfectly and never once understand.

He came home carrying memories that haunted him for years, and Navajo healing ceremonies helped put the young Marine back in balance. Through it all he said nothing — the code stayed classified until 1968. In 2001 he stood in the Capitol Rotunda as the President placed the Congressional Gold Medal around the original talkers' necks. His memoir, "Code Talker," told the story at last, and when Chester Nez died on June 4, 2014, at 93, the last of the legendary 29 went with him — but the code they built remains unbroken forever.

“It stings but it's nothing.” Most people might say that when describing a carpet burn or perhaps a bee sting. Staff Sgt. Viggiani, on the other hand, said that of a bullet wound sustained on June 3, 2004, in the mountainous region around Khabargho, Afghanistan.

His team and another squad received reports that a group of Taliban fighters were fleeing out of the town and into the forbidding hills – incredibly tough terrain full of caves and crevices, pits, and pitfalls.

As the men approached the ridgeline north of town, Viggiani's squad lost touch with the others as the mountains interfered with the radio transmissions. Then Viggiani and his squad came under heavy and accurate fire, which injured two Marines and halted the advance. Viggiani crept forward, as it seemed like the fire was coming from the steep slope in front of him.
Viggiani and another Marine continued their slow advance – and suddenly came under direct fire. Shooting was coming from a cave just a few feet away, and the enemies were still firing at the wounded Marines who had taken cover behind a nearby rock. With the rest of his team pinned down, it fell to Viggiani to eliminate the well-entrenched insurgents. Maneuvering to a better position, he found himself peering through a small break in the rocks. When he saw a piece of cloth move, he fired off three or four rounds. He heard no sounds that would lead him to believe the enemies had been hit, so he grabbed a grenade and dropped it into the hole. The cave blew apart, exposing three now-dead Taliban snipers.

With the threat eliminated, the medic was able to reach and treat the two injured Marines. Viggiani refused treatment on the gunshot to his leg, and instead continued fighting. After three or four hours of intense chase and fighting, the Marines killed 14 enemy fighters and cleared the area. For his leadership and bravery, Viggiani was awarded the Navy Cross on Jan. 25, 2006.

He spent his final days bringing his surrounded soldiers home. Sixty-two years later, his country finally brought him home. 🇺🇸

In November 1950, Lieutenant Colonel Don Carlos Faith Jr. commanded the 1st Battalion, 32nd Infantry Regiment, near the Chosin Reservoir in North Korea. Chinese forces had encircled the Americans in brutal winter cold — temperatures plunging, weapons jamming in the freeze, wounded men fighting simply to survive.

Faith refused to stay behind the lines. Again and again he exposed himself to enemy fire, directing his men and personally leading counterattacks. When his battered force linked up with another surrounded American unit, he took command of the combined group — the force history remembers as Task Force Faith — and led the desperate fight to break out toward friendly lines, roadblock after roadblock standing in the way.

On December 1, Faith led the assault on an enemy roadblock himself, advancing with his pistol and throwing grenades. Shrapnel tore into him, but he kept directing his men until the obstacle fell. He succumbed to his wounds the following day. In the chaos of the retreat, his body could not be recovered.

He was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor in 1951. His wife and his four-year-old daughter, Bobbie, accepted the decoration — with no grave to visit. In 2012, after decades of uncertainty, military specialists identified his remains through forensic evidence and DNA. On April 17, 2013, Don Faith was laid to rest with full military honors at Arlington National Cemetery. His daughter was there. He had spent his last days fighting to bring his soldiers home — and more than six decades later, his country finally brought him home.

Ashly Moyer deserves to be remembered not only for how she served, but for the future she never got to live — a daughter, a loved one, a young woman with everything still ahead of her.

In the Hanoi Hilton, the guards answered to their commanders. The prisoners answered to James Stockdale. 🇺🇸

When Commander James Stockdale's A-4 Skyhawk was shot down over North Vietnam on September 9, 1965, he became the highest-ranking American naval officer in captivity — and the leader of the prisoner resistance. From inside Hoa Lo Prison, Stockdale built an organization out of whispers and wall-taps: a code of conduct for men under torture, secret communications between cells, and one unbreakable rule — nobody cooperates, nobody bows, everybody comes home with honor.

The North Vietnamese isolated him for it: years in solitary, long stretches in leg irons in the punishment annex the POWs called Alcatraz. In 1969, chosen to be paraded in a propaganda film, Stockdale beat his own face with a stool and cut himself with a razor fragment rather than be used — he would be photographed battered or not at all. His captors understood the message: this man would die before he bent. In the aftermath, the worst of the torture campaign eased.

Stockdale came home in February 1973, pictured here descending from the aircraft a free man, and received the Medal of Honor in 1976. Eight years a prisoner, four of them in solitary — and the men he led credit his iron example with bringing them home alive, together, and unashamed. He died in 2005, an admiral, a philosopher of endurance, and the standard by which American POWs are still measured.

Commander Jeremiah Denton, a Navy A-6 Intruder pilot, was shot down over North Vietnam on July 18, 1965, and dragged into the prison system the Americans called the Hanoi Hilton. In May 1966, his captors sat him before Japanese television cameras for a propaganda interview, expecting a broken man to parrot their script.

Denton gave them the performance they wanted with his voice — while his eyes told a different story. As he spoke, he blinked, again and again, in Morse code: T-O-R-T-U-R-E. American intelligence officers studying the film caught it — the first proof the world had that American POWs were being tortured. It is one of the most extraordinary acts of defiance ever committed in front of an enemy's own camera.

Denton endured seven years and seven months of captivity, much of it in solitary and in the punishment camp the prisoners called Alcatraz, and came home in February 1973 — the first man off the plane at Clark Air Base, where he spoke for all of them: "We are honored to have had the opportunity to serve our country under difficult circumstances." He retired a Rear Admiral, served Alabama in the United States Senate, and died in 2014. The blink that outsmarted an empire still teaches every American service member what resistance means.

Starved to 98 pounds in a jungle prison, he crawled out of it — and then outran the jungle itself. 🇺🇸

Dieter Dengler grew up in the ruins of postwar Germany dreaming of American airplanes, crossed the ocean as a teenager, and earned his wings as a U.S. Navy pilot. On February 1, 1966, flying an A-1 Skyraider from the carrier Ranger on a secret mission over Laos, his plane was hit and crashed in the jungle. Dengler survived the crash — and walked straight into a Pathet Lao patrol.

What followed was months of torture: hung upside down, beaten, dragged, starved, staked to the ground in the camp as the prisoners wasted away. On June 29, 1966, the starving prisoners made their break. Dengler got out — one of only two of the escapees to survive the jungle — and then did the hardest part alone: 23 days evading recapture on foot, barefoot, eating what the wild offered, hiding from the men hunting him.

On July 20, 1966, an American Skyraider pilot spotted a signal on the jungle floor — a parachute laid out as an SOS by a man who refused to die — and helicopters pulled Dieter Dengler out, weighing less than 100 pounds, smiling for the cameras days later. He received the Navy Cross, flew again, and remains the only American airman to escape a Laotian prison camp and live to tell it.

He bombed Japan, rotted in its allies' cells for 40 months — then went back to Japan to love its people. 🇺🇸

Corporal Jacob DeShazer was the bombardier on the last plane of the Doolittle Raid, the daring carrier-launched strike on Tokyo of April 18, 1942. Out of fuel over occupied China, his crew bailed out into the night — straight into Japanese hands. Eight Raiders were captured; three were executed, one starved to death. DeShazer endured forty months of cells, hunger, disease and beatings, most of it in solitary confinement, not knowing if he would ever see Oregon again.

In that darkness, a smuggled Bible reached his cell — and DeShazer made a vow that sounds impossible: if he lived, he would return to Japan not with hatred, but as a missionary. He lived. Freed in August 1945, he kept the vow: in 1948 Jacob DeShazer went back to Japan and spent thirty years preaching to the people who had caged him.

A pamphlet telling his story fell into the hands of Mitsuo Fuchida — the commander who led the attack on Pearl Harbor. It helped change Fuchida's life; the two former enemies met, shook hands, and became friends. Jacob DeShazer died in 2008 at 95 — a POW who answered torture with the most disarming weapon ever carried into a prison camp: forgiveness.

In a historic ruling, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit struck down core provisions of the 1958 Federal Switchblade Act, holding that automatically opening knives qualify as protected "Arms" under the plain text of the Second Amendment.

Dismantling a 1950s Ban: Enacted in 1958 amid 1950s pop-culture panics over juvenile delinquency, Section 1242 of the Federal Switchblade Act made it a federal crime to manufacture, transport, or sell automatic knives across state lines. The appellate panel found that the federal government failed to demonstrate any historical tradition justifying an interstate commercial ban.

Knives Are Constitutionally Protected "Arms": Applying the Supreme Court's historical-tradition framework, Chief Judge Jennifer Walker Elrod wrote for the panel that bladed tools have been used for self-defense throughout American history. The court explicitly held that the right to keep and bear arms necessarily includes the right to manufacture, ship, and acquire them through interstate commerce.

What Changes (and What Doesn't): While the decision represents a major victory for pro-knife advocacy groups like Knife Rights and clears federal interstate trade barriers within the circuit, it does not automatically override individual state or municipal concealed-carry and blade-length statutes, which remain governed under separate local laws.

They called him unbroken — and after 47 days at sea and two years in the camps, the name fit. 🇺🇸

Louis Zamperini was an Olympic runner from California who raced at the 1936 Berlin Games, and when war came he became a bombardier on a B-24 over the Pacific. On May 27, 1943, his crippled bomber, the Green Hornet, fell into the ocean during a rescue search. Zamperini and two crewmates survived on a tiny raft — drinking rain, catching fish and birds, fending off sharks — for 47 days, among the longest sea survivals in history. One of the three died on the raft. The other two washed up alive — straight into Japanese hands.

What followed was worse than the ocean: more than two years in prisoner-of-war camps, singled out for torment by a sadistic guard the prisoners called "the Bird," who beat the famous Olympian with a belt, starved him, and tried to break the thing in him that would not bend. It never broke. Zamperini came home in 1945 carrying nightmares that nearly destroyed him with drink — until, by his own account, faith put him back together, and the man who had every reason to hate flew back to Japan to forgive his captors face to face.

He died in 2014 at 97, a torch-bearer, a mentor to generations of young men, and the subject of the book and film "Unbroken." The title is not poetry. It is a description.

Lance Corporal Joshua Moore occupied a hide near Marjah, Afghanistan, with several other scout snipers when their position came under attack. Two Marines right outside the structure fell wounded. Suddenly, Moore felt something bounce off his back. He turned and found two enemy grenades on the floor. Without hesitation, Moore picked up one and threw it out the door, where the grenade safely exploded away from the Marines. As he grabbed the second grenade to throw back, he realized it was corroded and defective. Moore then ran outside into the enemy fire to help the wounded. Using his M4 and grenade launcher, Moore neutralized the enemy position 100 meters away while others moved the casualties to safety. Moore then helped clear a LZ for medevac.

For his heroic actions, at risk to his own life, two years later Moore was awarded the Navy Cross. He had been promoted to Sergeant by the time of the award.

“...serving with Scout Sniper Platoon, Second Battalion, Eighth Marines, on 14 March 2011 in support of Operation ENDURING FREEDOM. LCpl Moore demonstrated audacity and selfless devotion to duty in the face of a determined enemy when his element came under attack north of Marjah. Two Marines who were outside the structure the team was using for cover immediately became casualties. Insurgents then threw two grenades over the wall into the team's position. Without hesitation and with complete disregard for his own life, LCpl Moore picked up the first grenade and threw it out of the building, where it immediately detonated. He then picked up the second grenade, recognized it had malfunctioned and would not detonate, discarded it, and charged out of the structure to aid the wounded. Though instantly taken under fire by an enemy force one hundred meters away, LCpl Moore stood his ground, returning fire with his M-4 rifle and M-203 grenade launcher. The effects of his fire neutralized the enemy and forced them to abandon their position, buying his team time to regroup and aid their wounded. He then immediately took action to assist in securing a landing zone to extract wounded personnel.”

On a little hill in Pennsylvania, a professor gave an order that saved the Union — and his little brother stood beside him. 🇺🇸

Joshua Lawrence Chamberlain, pictured here, was a Bowdoin College professor of rhetoric who spoke ten languages and had no military training when he talked his way into the Army. By July 2, 1863, he commanded the 20th Maine — and held the extreme left end of the entire Union line on Little Round Top at Gettysburg, with orders to hold "to the last." Among the officers beside him was his younger brother, Lieutenant Thomas Chamberlain.

All afternoon the 20th Maine beat back wave after wave of Alabamians climbing the rocks. Then the ammunition ran out. What Joshua did next is studied in war colleges to this day: he fixed bayonets and ordered a downhill charge — the line swinging like a gate — that swept the stunned Confederates off the hill and, many historians believe, saved the Army of the Potomac. He was wounded so often in that war that newspapers printed his obituary by mistake; Grant chose him to formally receive the Confederate surrender at Appomattox, where Chamberlain ordered his men to salute their defeated enemies as they stacked their arms.

Thomas did not live to see the peace — disease, the silent k*ller of every Civil War camp, claimed him in 1864. Joshua carried his brother's memory through fifty more years: governor, college president, and the old soldier whose name still means Little Round Top.

Can modern forensic breakthroughs finally bring closure to families more than five decades after one of America's most notorious serial killers struck?

Summit County, Utah prosecutors and law enforcement officials have formally linked infamous serial killer Ted Bundy to the unsolved October 1974 murder of 17-year-old Melissa Ann Smith through advanced DNA testing.

A 52-Year Cold Case Solved: Melissa Ann Smith disappeared in late October 1974, and her body was later discovered in Summit County by hunters. For decades, her murder remained officially unsolved despite long-standing suspicions regarding Bundy's presence in Utah while attending law school.

The Forensics Breakthrough: Investigators closed the case after connecting genetic evidence preserved from Smith's autopsy to DNA profiles established in the case of Laura Aime—another 17-year-old Utah victim whose murder was definitively tied to Bundy through DNA earlier this year.

Closing the Book on Unsolved Victims: Executed in Florida's electric chair in 1989, Bundy confessed to dozens of killings across Washington, Utah, Colorado, Idaho, and Florida, though several remained unconfirmed. Utah investigators emphasized that every cold case closure helps bring answers to surviving families while bringing permanent resolution to his trail of crimes.

Two brothers of one Wisconsin family — and between them, two of the Civil War's most impossible feats. 🇺🇸

Alonzo Cushing, pictured here, was a 22-year-old artillery lieutenant whose battery stood at the very center of the Union line at Gettysburg — the stone wall called the Angle — on July 3, 1863. As Pickett's Charge rolled toward him, Alonzo was wounded again and again: a shell fragment through the shoulder, another through the body. Ordered to the rear, he refused, had himself held upright beside his last serviceable gun, and was sighting it with his thumb over the vent when a bullet struck him down at his post. The charge broke on the ground he would not leave. In November 2014 — 151 years later — President Barack Obama placed Alonzo Cushing's Medal of Honor where it had always belonged.

His younger brother needed no land battle for his legend. William Barker Cushing of the U.S. Navy, on the night of October 27, 1864, steamed a tiny launch with a spar torpedo up the dark Roanoke River, alone past Confederate guards, and detonated it beneath the ironclad CSS Albemarle — sinking the South's most feared warship and swimming for his life through icy water as it went down.

One brother held the line at the war's turning point. The other sank an ironclad in the dark. America has rarely asked more of one family's sons — and never received more.

One family. Six months. Four telegrams. 🇺🇸

Alben and Gunda Borgstrom, a farming couple from Thatcher, Utah, sent their sons to war one after another. In 1944, the telegrams began to arrive — and they did not stop.

First came word of Clyde, a Marine on Guadalcanal, lost in March 1944. Then LeRoy, a soldier, gone in the fighting in the summer of 1944. Then Rolon, lost in France. Then Rulon, an airman, missing over Europe and declared d*ad. Four brothers, lost within six months — in the Pacific and in Europe, on the sea of war's every front — while their parents kept the farm and their faith and waited for news of the boys who remained.

What was left of the family's strength, the military itself moved to protect: their fifth serving son, Boyd, was ordered home out of harm's way, released from further combat service so the Borgstrom line would not be extinguished entirely — one of the cases that hardened America's resolve to protect sole surviving sons.

In June 1948, the Army brought the four brothers home together. Thousands gathered in Utah as Clyde, LeRoy, Rolon and Rulon were laid to rest side by side in the Thatcher cemetery — four white markers, one unbearable row, and a nation's debt written in a single family's names.

FORT BENNING, Ga. (USASOC News Service, Dec. 2, 2009) -- A squad leader with the 75th Ranger Regiment was awarded the Silver Star for risking his life to save two fellow Rangers in Afghanistan.

"Any Ranger would have done the same thing," said Staff Sgt. Michael E. Norton of Alpha Company, 3rd Battalion, 75th Rangers. "The Ranger Creed says, 'I will never leave a fallen comrade.' There was no moment of thinking about what to do. I had to get my brothers, and the most important thing in my mind was how hurt they were."

Norton led his squad on an objective, Aug. 4-5, to raid an enemy combatant's headquarters camp in the mountains of northwestern Khowst Province in Afghanistan.

While moving to the objective, Norton and one of his team leaders were alerted to possible enemy combatants along the route and moved forward to assess the situation. As Norton and his team leader were attempting to identify the possible enemy in the valley, a seven—to nine-man enemy element initiated a complex, near ambush on Norton's squad from the high ground with rocket-propelled grenades and small arms fire from a position 25 meters to the squad's front.
"The fire came from our 12 o'clock and then maybe a couple of seconds later from our right and left," Norton said.

Behind the first enemy rocket-propelled grenade team, a medium machine gun on elevated ground to the northwest engaged them with highly effective fire. Two more enemy combatants were on the slope of the valley to the west, engaged the Ranger squad with an AK-47 and rocket-propelled grenades along the long axis of their formation, while another group of enemy fighters were on elevated terrain to the east, raked them with small arms fire from the rear of the Ranger squad formation.

The multiple enemy positions had effectively enveloped Norton's squad from multiple directions at a distance of 25 to 50 meters, leaving Norton and his element pinned to the floor of the valley by the intense and accurate small arms fire.

The valley left no room for maneuver; Norton, his squad and the machine gun team element behind them immediately returned fire, but they were unable to gain fire superiority over the well-established enemy.

After the second rocket-propelled grenades knocked two of his Rangers temporarily unconscious and blasted the rest of his squad with shrapnel and debris and realizing his element could not gain fire superiority, Norton shouted for his squad to break contact.

When Norton realized that two Rangers had not gotten up and were still exposed to the heavy volume of enemy fire from the high ground to the east and west, and with complete disregard for his own safety, Norton turned around and with marked distinction, purposefully charged back into the interlocking fire of the enemy ambush kill zone in order to recover his downed Rangers.

"The example of personal courage that Staff Sergeant Norton showed, to get his men out of the kill zone is a testament to his character," said Maj. Keith Carter, A Company commander. "NCOs such as Staff Sergeant Norton are the reason I wanted to serve in the 75th Ranger Regiment, and it is an honor to lead them."

Without hesitation, Norton dove down into the midst of enemy fire with his unconscious comrades, uncertain of their status.

"There was nothing fancy going on in my head besides hoping they weren't dead," said Norton.

While the rest of the element attempted to suppress the enemy, and lying next to the Rangers, Norton "started shaking and yelling as quietly as I could."

After reviving his Rangers, Norton led them back to cover through the hail of direct fire and rocket-propelled grenade strikes, saving their lives and bringing his entire squad out of the enemy onslaught intact.

"I'm proud of the actions of my squad, because we continued the mission after that," said Norton. "It was just two minutes out of our overall mission."

As his platoon fought off the enemy ambush with direct fire, mortars and close air support, Norton quickly assessed his casualties and reorganized his squad to return to the fight.

Norton continued leading his squad in the follow-on assaults through two more direct fire contacts, killing two enemy combatants.

"We receive a lot of great training here at 3rd Ranger Battalion and I was just acting on instinct," said Norton.

The training conducted by Rangers means everything on the battlefield.

"The goal of the company and battalion is to create the most realistic scenarios possible while minimizing risk," Carter said. We constantly integrate new enemy tactics from overseas into our training so that we are ready in any situation."

The overall assault force killed 20 enemy fighters and destroyed two enemy anti-aircraft guns and several other weapons, explosives, and military supplies on the objective, disrupting a major enemy headquarters and encampment.

Norton joined the Army from his hometown of Pensacola, Fla., June 2004, after graduating from West Highland Christian Academy, and has deployed six times in support of operations Enduring and Iraqi Freedom. He is the son of Jimmy and Deborah Norton of Holly, Mich.

This is the true story behind Saving Private Ryan — and the truth is harder than the film. 🇺🇸

Four brothers from Tonawanda, New York, went to war: Edward, Preston, Robert and Frederick "Fritz" Niland. In one terrible June of 1944, the family's world collapsed. Robert, a paratrooper of the 82nd Airborne, was k*lled on D-Day itself at Neuville-au-Plain. The very next day, June 7, Preston, also a paratrooper, fell near Utah Beach. And from the other side of the world came word that Edward, an airman whose plane had gone down in the Burmese jungle, was missing and presumed d*ad.

That left Fritz, fighting with the 101st Airborne in Normandy. When the Army realized three brothers were gone, it moved fast: the regimental chaplain, Father Francis Sampson, tracked Fritz down and the last Niland son was pulled from the line and sent home to his mother — the real "sole survivor" mission that Steven Spielberg later transformed into Saving Private Ryan.

And then, in 1945, came the telegram no one dared hope for: Edward was alive. Emaciated in a Japanese prison camp, he had survived. Two Niland brothers came home. Two rest side by side today in the American cemetery above Normandy — Preston and Robert, together, under white crosses in Plot B.

Five brothers. One ship. One night that changed America's rules of war forever. 🇺🇸

George, Francis, Joseph, Madison and Albert Sullivan were five Irish-American brothers from Waterloo, Iowa. When their friend Bill Ball was k*lled aboard the USS Arizona at Pearl Harbor, the brothers enlisted together — with one condition the Navy granted: they would serve together. All five were posted to the light cruiser USS Juneau, and their smiling photograph aboard her became one of the famous images of the young war.

On the night of November 13, 1942, in the savage naval battles off Guadalcanal, a Japanese torpedo struck the Juneau's magazine. She disintegrated and sank in less than a minute. Some hundred men survived the sinking and clung to rafts in shark-haunted water — but through a chain of communication failures, no rescue came for days. When help finally arrived, only ten men were pulled out alive. All five Sullivan brothers were gone.

Their mother Alleta received the news with a grace that humbled a nation, and their sister Genevieve joined the Navy's WAVES in their honor. The Navy named a destroyer USS The Sullivans — the only American warship ever named for a family — and the tragedy drove the military to separate siblings and protect sole surviving sons. "We stick together" was the brothers' motto. They did — to the very end.

Before there was a 75th Ranger Regiment, there was one young colonel in Scotland, building America's first Rangers from scratch. 🇺🇸

In the spring of 1942, with America reeling from defeats, Major William Orlando Darby — just 31 years old — was given a mission: create an American unit modeled on the legendary British Commandos. Five hundred volunteers were selected and shipped to Achnacarry, Scotland, where Commando instructors ran them through a course so brutal it used live ammunition. On June 19, 1942, the 1st Ranger Battalion was born — and Darby's men, pictured training here in those early days, were its standard-bearers.

That November, Rangers spearheaded the landings in North Africa, paddling ashore in darkness to silence the guns of Arzew. They fought through Sicily and Italy, at Gela and Salerno and Anzio — and at Cisterna, in January 1944, the 1st and 3rd Ranger Battalions walked into an ambush and were nearly annihilated: of 767 men who went in, only six came back.

Darby refused a safe job in Washington and returned to his men in Italy. On April 30, 1945, days before the war in Europe ended, a shell fragment took his life; he was promoted to Brigadier General on the day of his death. Today's Rangers still carry his name, his scroll, and his challenge — Darby's challenge — to lead the way. Rangers Lead The Way.

On this day, 84 years ago, October 27, 1942, 42-year-old Temporary Lieutenant-Colonel Victor Buller Turner commanded the 2nd Battalion, The Rifle Brigade at a position designated Outpost Snipe during the Second Battle of El Alamein.

His battalion had navigated through enemy minefields overnight to occupy a shallow desert depression near Kidney Ridge, only to find themselves completely isolated at daybreak.

Turner came from a family with a distinct military heritage.

His older brother, Second Lieutenant Alexander Buller Turner, had received a posthumous Victoria Cross in 1915 during the First World War, making them one of only four pairs of brothers in history to win Britain's highest military honor.

He was also related to General Sir Redvers Buller, who earned the Victoria Cross during the Anglo-Zulu War in 1879.

At Outpost Snipe, Turner's force of roughly 300 men with nineteen 6-pounder anti-tank guns faced armored elements of the German 15th and 21st Panzer Divisions and the Italian Ariete Armoured Division.

Axis forces surrounded the position and launched relentless armored counter-attacks with over ninety tanks and self-propelled guns throughout the day.

The desert heat topped 100 degrees Fahrenheit as continuous artillery, mortar, and machine-gun fire rained down into the shallow depression.

Turner moved constantly between his forward anti-tank gun pits on foot to direct fire and keep his men organized under direct shellfire.

Targeting German Panzer III and IV tanks, the gun crews held their fire until enemy armor closed within 100 yards to ensure maximum penetration.

As casualties mounted, several 6-pounder anti-tank guns were left unmanned or severely shorthanded.

When one vital gun pit was stripped of its crew except for an officer and a sergeant, Turner ran across open, bullet-swept ground to join them.

He immediately stepped into the role of loader, hauling heavy 6-pounder solid-shot shells and jamming them into the breech.

Exposed from the waist up to direct machine-gun and tank cannon fire, Turner loaded round after round as the crew engaged German armor at point-blank range.

Together, this single gun crew destroyed five German tanks at a distance of less than 50 yards before the attack stalled.

While carrying ammunition shells to keep the gun operational, a high-explosive shell burst nearby, spraying shrapnel into Turner's head.

The fragment inflicted a severe scalp wound that bled heavily down his face and neck.

Turner refused medical evacuation, brushed off aid, and remained on his feet at the forward perimeter to direct the remaining guns.

By the time the battle ended, Turner's battalion had destroyed or disabled 37 enemy tanks and self-propelled guns, shattering the Axis armored counter-offensive.

King George VI presented Turner with the Victoria Cross at Buckingham Palace on July 27, 1943.

After the war, Turner remained in the British Army and retired with the rank of Lieutenant-Colonel.

He was later appointed to the Royal Household as a Yeoman of the Guard in 1950.

In 1966, he was made a Commander of the Royal Victorian Order, and in 1967 he became Lieutenant of the Queen's Bodyguard of the Yeomen of the Guard.

Victor Buller Turner died on August 7, 1972, at the age of 72 in Ditchingham, Norfolk, and his Victoria Cross is currently displayed at the Royal Green Jackets Museum in Winchester.

The enemy kept a diary about them. One word appears again and again: the Black Devils. 🇺🇸

The First Special Service Force was an experiment no army had tried: one elite unit of Americans and Canadians, mixed together, trained for everything — parachuting, skiing, mountain climbing, amphibious raids, demolitions — at a secret camp in Montana under Colonel Robert Frederick.

In December 1943, at Monte la Difensa in Italy, the Force did what Allied planners called impossible: in a freezing night rainstorm, its men scaled a sheer cliff the Germans had left undefended precisely because no one could climb it — and took the summit fortress in two hours. At the Anzio beachhead, they owned the night: faces blackened, slipping into German lines to raid, sabotage and vanish, leaving behind their red spearhead sticker and a calling card in German: "Das dicke Ende kommt noch!" — "The worst is yet to come!"

A captured German officer's diary gave them their immortal name, describing an enemy that struck invisibly in the dark: "the Black Devils." The Force was disbanded in December 1944, its ranks shattered by casualties — but both nations' special forces trace their bloodline to it. The Devil's Brigade never lost a battle it was sent to win.

Can Ukrainian frontline units hold the line as the Pokrovsk sector erupts into one of the most violently contested axes of the entire war?

According to daily operational updates from the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Ukrainian defenders repelled 36 Russian assaults in the Pokrovsk sector alone, amid a relentless operational surge that recorded 177 combat clashes across the front line in a single 24-hour period.

The Pokrovsk direction continues to absorb the heaviest concentration of adversary armored thrusts and infantry assaults, as Russian forces press aggressively to compromise vital logistical lifelines in Donetsk Oblast.

Despite heavy artillery preparatory bombardments, guided glide bombs (KABs), and continuous mechanized waves, Ukrainian artillery, anti-tank teams, and FPV drone operators successfully blunted all 36 targeted assault vectors.

While the Pokrovsk sector remains the hottest contact zone on the map, intense localized fighting also stretched defenders across the Lyman, Kostiantynivka, and Huliaipole fronts, underscoring the grueling operational tempo spanning hundreds of miles.

America locked their families behind barbed wire — then these sons volunteered to fight for it. 🇺🇸

After Pearl Harbor, more than 120,000 Japanese Americans were forced from their homes into internment camps. And from inside those camps, thousands of their sons stepped forward and volunteered for the United States Army. They became the 442nd Regimental Combat Team — fighting under a motto in Hawaiian pidgin: "Go For Broke."

In Italy and France, the 442nd built a legend battle by battle. In October 1944, in the freezing Vosges Mountains, they smashed through German lines to rescue the "Lost Battalion" — 211 trapped Texans of the 141st Infantry — at a cost of some 800 casualties of their own. Their artillerymen, like the 522nd Field Artillery gunners pictured here under their camouflage net, were famed for speed and precision — and in the spring of 1945, men of the 522nd were among the liberators who reached the sub-camps of Dachau.

For its size and length of service, the 442nd became the most decorated unit in United States Army history: more than 18,000 individual decorations, including 21 Medals of Honor. They had set out to prove their loyalty to a country that doubted it. They ended up proving something greater — what loyalty actually looks like.

The U.S. Navy embraces Castelion's low-cost "Blackbeard" hypersonic missile to counter complex anti-access/area-denial (A2/AD) networks.

As defense leaders shift focus toward high-end conventional deterrence in the Indo-Pacific, the U.S. military is rapidly accelerating the development and fielding of mass-producible, high-speed strike weapons designed to outpace adversary defensive perimeters.

 Developed by defense startup Castelion, the Blackbeard (selected under the Navy's Multi-mission Affordable Capacity Effector or MACE initiative) is an air-launched, long-range hypersonic weapon capable of speeds exceeding Mach 4 to Mach 5-plus.

 Unlike multi-million-dollar legacy hypersonics, Blackbeard is engineered specifically for mass production, with initial pre-production batches priced around $468,000 and long-term targets aiming under $300,000 per unit.

 Designed to integrate seamlessly with carrier air wings aboard platforms like the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and F-35, the weapon allows strike fighters to hold high-value mobile and time-sensitive targets at risk from far outside adversary A2/AD missile engagement zones.
